verses.zh: 伯沙撒王在位第三年，有异象现与我―但以理，是在先前所见的异象之后。
verses.en: [NOTE:1] In the third year[NOTE:2] of King Belshazzar’s reign, a vision appeared to me, Daniel, after the one that had appeared to me previously.[NOTE:3]
notes: Dan 8:1 marks the switch from Aramaic (= 2:4b-7:28) back to Hebrew as the language in which the book is written in its present form. The remainder of the book from this point on (8:1-12:13) is in Hebrew. The bilingual nature of the book has been variously explained, but it most likely has to do with the book’s transmission history; see the note at 2:4.
The third year of King Belshazzar’s reign would have been ca. 551 b.c. Daniel would have been approximately 69 years old at the time of this vision.
Heb “in the beginning.” This refers to the vision described in chapter seven.
verses.commentary:
8:1 "In the third year of the reign of Belshazzar" This shows that the vision of chapter 8 came
after a time span of two years from the vision of chapter 7. We do not know when or how long Belshazzar
served as co-regent under his father, Nabonidus, before the fall of the Neo-Babylon Empire by the army of
Cyrus II, known as Cyrus the Great (cf. Daniel 5). Chapter 8 restarts the Hebrew section of the book of Daniel
(i.e., Dan. 1:1-2:3; 8:1-12:13).

▣ "vision" In chapters 2 and 4 Daniel receives from God the interpretation of dreams that Nebuchadnezzar II had, but in
chapters 7; 8; 10; 11, he is directly addressed by God in his own vision. In chapter 7:1, this divine revelation is called both "a dream" and
"a vision." In Daniel there seems to be no distinction made between these two means of revelation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

▣

NASB
"previously"

NKJV
"the first time"

NRSV, Peshitta
"at first"

TEV
"I saw a second vision"

NJB
"originally"

REB
"my earlier vision"

JPSOA
"appeared to me earlier"

LXX
"the first one"

This is literally "at the first" (BDB 321, e.g., 9:21; Gen. 13:3; 2 Sam. 21:9,10;
2 Kgs. 17:25; Neh. 11:17), which is idiomatic for the vision Daniel received earlier in Belshazzar's
reign (i.e., Daniel 7).

verses.zh: 我见了异象的时候，我以为在以拦省书珊城（或译：宫）中；我见异象又如在乌莱河边。
verses.en: In this[NOTE:1] vision I saw myself in Susa[NOTE:2] the citadel,[NOTE:3] which is located in the province of Elam. In the vision I saw myself at the Ulai Canal.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “the.”

Susa (Heb. שׁוּשַׁן, shushan), located some 230 miles (380 km) east of Babylon, was a winter residence for Persian kings during the Achaemenid period. The language of v. 2 seems to suggest that Daniel may not have been physically present at Susa, but only saw himself there in the vision. However, the Hebrew is difficult, and some have concluded that the first four words of v. 2 in the MT are a later addition (cf. Theodotion).

The Hebrew word בִּירָה (birah, “castle, palace”) usually refers to a fortified structure within a city, but here it is in apposition to the city name Susa and therefore has a broader reference to the entire city (against this view, however, see BDB 108 s.v. 2). Cf. NAB “the fortress of Susa”; TEV “the walled city of Susa.”

The term אוּבַל (ʾuval = “stream, river”) is a relatively rare word in biblical Hebrew, found only here and in vv. 3 and 6. The Ulai was apparently a sizable artificial canal in Susa (cf. NASB, NIV, NCV) and not a river in the ordinary sense of that word.
verses.commentary:
8:2 "I was in the citadel of Susa" Susa later became the capitol of the kingdom of Persia
(cf. Neh. 1:1); but at this time it was simply a large, fortified city in the province of Elam
(i.e., east of the Tigris River, cf. Isa. 22:6; Jer. 49:34-39). It would later be called Shushan
(cf. Neh. 1:1; Esther 1:2,5). The Greek name was Susa.

Was Daniel physically in Susa, or was this part of the vision? He could have been in Susa
on governmental business (cf. Dan. 8:27). There seems to be no integral part of the vision linked to this
locality.

Several visions in the Bible involve some type of mental or physical transport.

- Ezekiel, from Babylon, to the temple in Jerusalem, Ezek. 8 (cf. Ezek. 3:14; 11:1; 43:5)

- Philip, in Gaza, taken to Azotus, Acts 8:39-40

- John, on Patmos, taken to heaven, Rev. 4:2 (cf. Rev. 17:3; 21:10)

▣ "I looked in the vision, and I myself was" Daniel sees himself in his vision for the first time.

▣ "Ulai Canal" This was a 900 foot wide man made irrigation canal north of the city (BDB 19 I), which
connected two rivers. The ancient Bible versions in Greek, Aramaic, and Latin translate this rare Hebrew word
"canal" or "river" (BDB 385).

verses.zh: 我举目观看，见有双角的公绵羊站在河边，两角都高。这角高过那角，更高的是后长的。
verses.en: I looked up[NOTE:1] and saw[NOTE:2] a[NOTE:3] ram with two horns standing at the canal. Its two horns were both long,[NOTE:4] but one was longer than the other. The longer one was coming up after the shorter one.
notes: Heb “lifted my eyes.”
Heb “saw and behold.”
Heb “one.” The Hebrew numerical adjective occasionally functions like an English indefinite article. See GKC 401 §125.b.
Heb “high” (also “higher” later in this verse).
verses.commentary:
8:3 "a ram which had two horns" This seems to refer to Medo-Persia (cf. Dan. 8:20) and is analogous to
the bear with one side lifted of Daniel 7 and the breast and arms of silver in chapter 2.

The horns are described by several features.

- two horns

- one longer than the other

- the longer one came up after the other was in place

They probably represent the historical fact that Cyrus (1/2 Median descent) first conquered Media
and then later became the king of Persia after the fall of Neo-Babylon. The two horns may also be parallel
to the bear of chapter 7, raised on one side (showing the dominant kingdom of Persia in the Medo-Persian
Empire (cf. Dan. 8:20). See chart in Contextual Insights, A., B.

verses.zh: 我见那公绵羊往西、往北、往南抵触。兽在它面前都站立不住，也没有能救护脱离它手的；但它任意而行，自高自大。
verses.en: I saw that the ram was butting westward, northward, and southward. No animal[NOTE:1] was able to stand before it, and there was none who could deliver from its power.[NOTE:2] It did as it pleased and acted arrogantly.[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “beast” (NAB).
Heb “hand,” as also in v. 7.

In the Hiphil the Hebrew verb גָּדַל (gadal, “to make great; to magnify”) can have either a positive or a negative sense. For the former, used especially of God, see Ps 126:2, 3 and Joel 2:21. In this chapter (8:4, 8, 11, 25) the word has a pejorative sense, describing the self-glorification of this king. The sense seems to be that of vainly assuming one’s own superiority through deliberate hubris.
verses.commentary:
8:4 "I saw the ram butting westward, northward and southward " Many use this as parallel to the
three ribs in the bear's mouth, Dan. 7:5, to describe the three directions of Medo-Persian conquest.

The nations that Greece conquered by compass direction were:

- westward ‒ Neo-Babylon, Syria, and Asia Minor

- northward ‒ Armenia and the area of the Caspian Sea

- southward ‒ Egypt and Ethiopia

▣ "nor was there anyone to rescue from his power; but he did as he pleased and magnified
himself" There are several aspects to this phrase that characterize the arrogance of these
Gentile kings and kingdoms (i.e., "no rescue," cf. Dan. 8:8,11,25).

- They thought no nation, army, or god could thwart their desires (i.e., "rescue," cf. Dan. 2:21).

- The essence of human rebellion is "I did it my way" ("he did as he pleased," Dan. 8:4,7).

- The king magnified himself (like the little horns of chapters 7 and 8), which attracts
God's notice and judgment (this phrase could be understood as relating to the power and
size of his kingdom as in Dan. 8:9, but this Hebrew word (BDB 152) has a negative connotation
in this chapter).

- He did as he pleased, which is a recurrent theme (cf. Dan. 5:19; 11:3,16,36-37).

This prediction is a good place to remind all interpreters of the fuzzy nature of
apocalyptic literature. The details are often for effect, not to be interpreted as literal historic events (cf. D. Brent Sandy,
Plowshares & Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic,
pp. 117-128). In fact, Greece did repel Persia's advance several times (490 B.C. and
480 B.C.). Apocalyptic literature cannot be interpreted or evaluated by the details. Often,
which of the details have significance can only be known after the fulfillment in history!

verses.zh: 我正思想的时候，见有一只公山羊从西而来，遍行全地，脚不沾尘。这山羊两眼当中有一非常的角。
verses.en: While I was contemplating all this,[NOTE:1] a male goat[NOTE:2] was coming from the west over the surface of all the land[NOTE:3] without touching the ground. This goat had a conspicuous horn[NOTE:4] between its eyes.
notes: The words “all this” are added in the translation for stylistic reasons and for clarification.
Heb “and behold, a he-goat of the goats.”
Or “of the whole earth” (NAB, ASV, NASB, NRSV).
Heb “a horn of vision” [or “conspicuousness”], i.e., “a conspicuous horn,” one easily seen.
verses.commentary:
8:5 "a male goat was coming from the west over the surface of the whole earth without touching
the ground" This refers to Greece (cf. Dan. 8:21; 11:3). Notice the speed of the victory (334-331
B.C.) and direction from which Alexander III, known as Alexander the Great, came. This
parallels the leopard with four wings of Dan. 7:6.

▣ "the surface of the whole earth" This is a hyperbolic statement which refers to the known
world of that day.

▣ "a conspicuous horn between his eyes" This refers to Alexander III, known as Alexander
the Great, who conquered the whole known world and died at the age of 32 (cf. Dan. 8:8,21-22; 11:4).

The term "conspicuous" (BDB 303) is very similar to the term "vision" (BDB 302) in Dan. 8:1.
In Isaiah it is used for a vision or oracle several times (cf. Isa. 21:2; 29:11). It means "conspicuous"
only in this context (Dan. 8:5,8).

verses.zh: 它往我所看见、站在河边有双角的公绵羊那里去，大发忿怒，向它直闯。
verses.en: It came to the two-horned ram that I had seen standing beside the canal and rushed against it with raging strength.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “the wrath of its strength.”
verses.commentary:
8:6-7 "rushed at him in his mighty wrath. . .and he was enraged at him" We know that Persia, under
Darius III, attacked Greece several times over the Hellespont (490 and 480 B.C.). This made
Greece so angry that when Alexander III finally crossed this narrow gap of water in 334 B.C.
with thirty thousand soldiers and five thousand cavalry, he engaged the Persian army with over 600,000 soldiers
and soundly defeated them several different times. Alexander would not make a peace treaty with Persia!

If one reads Daniel 8 alone, he would expect one decisive battle, but in fact, there were
three major decisive battles. The prediction is true, but fuzzy (as are all apocalyptic details, see note
at Dan. 8:4).

verses.zh: 我见公山羊就近公绵羊，向它发烈怒，抵触它，折断它的两角。绵羊在它面前站立不住；它将绵羊触倒在地，用脚践踏，没有能救绵羊脱离它手的。
verses.en: I saw it approaching the ram. It went into a fit of rage against the ram[NOTE:1] and struck it[NOTE:2] and broke off its two horns. The ram had no ability to resist it.[NOTE:3] The goat hurled the ram[NOTE:4] to the ground and trampled it. No one could deliver the ram from its power.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “him.”
Heb “the ram.”
Heb “stand before him.”
Heb “he hurled him.” The referents of both pronouns (the male goat and the ram) have been specified in the translation for clarity.

The goat of Daniel’s vision represents Greece; the large horn represents Alexander the Great. The ram stands for Media-Persia. Alexander’s rapid conquest of the Persians involved three battles of major significance that he won against overwhelming odds: Granicus (334 b.c.), Isus (333 b.c.), and Gaugemela (331 b.c.).

verses.zh: 这山羊极其自高自大，正强盛的时候，那大角折断了，又在角根上向天的四方（原文是风）长出四个非常的角来。
verses.en: The male goat acted even more arrogantly. But no sooner had the large horn become strong than it was broken, and there arose four conspicuous horns[NOTE:1] in its place,[NOTE:2] extending toward the four winds of the sky.[NOTE:3]
notes: The word “horns” is not in the Hebrew text but is implied.

The four conspicuous horns refer to Alexander’s successors. After his death, Alexander’s empire was divided up among four of his generals: Cassander, who took Macedonia and Greece; Lysimachus, who took Thrace and parts of Asia Minor; Seleucus, who took Syria and territory to its east; and Ptolemy, who took control of Egypt.
Or “the heavens.” The Hebrew term שָׁמַיִם (shamayim) may be translated “heavens” or “sky” depending on the context.
verses.commentary:
8:8 "the male goat magnified himself exceedingly" See note at Dan. 8:4,5.

▣ "the large horn was broken and in its place came up four conspicuous horns toward the four
winds of heaven" This refers to the death of Alexander the Great (323 B.C.) in Babylon
at the age of 32 or 33 caused by swamp fever. The unexpected, sudden death of Alexander caused great
and prolonged conflict throughout his kingdom. The governors or generals who were dominant as separate
regional satraps throughout his kingdom continued to maintain their control.

- Peucestas in Persia

- Peithon in Media

- Ptolemy in Egypt

- Lysimachus in Thrace

- Antigonus in Phrygia

- Leonnatus in Hellespontine

- Laomedon in Syria

- Lumenus in Cappadocia

- Stasonor in Bactria

- Philotas in Cilicia

- Asander in Lycia

- Menander in Lydia

The ones that impacted the Jews were #3 and #7, which are discussed in detail in Daniel 11.

I agree with E. J. Young that the "four conspicuous horns toward the four winds of heaven"
may be an idiom of universal rule not relating specifically to any of the four major generals. Apocalyptic literature
is designed to give an emotional general impression, not detailed facts of history. For a good discussion of the biblical
use of the number "four," see:

- SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN
SCRIPTURE, #2

- NIDOTTE, vol. 1, pp. 495-496

- Biblical Numerology by John J. Davis

verses.zh: 四角之中有一角长出一个小角，向南、向东、向荣美之地，渐渐成为强大。
verses.en: From one of them came a small horn,[NOTE:1] but it grew to be very great toward the south and the east and toward the beautiful land.[NOTE:2]
notes: This small horn is Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who controlled the Seleucid kingdom from ca. 175-164 b.c. Antiochus was extremely hostile toward the Jews and persecuted them mercilessly.
The expression the beautiful land (Heb. הַצֶּבִי [hatsevi] = “the beauty”) is a cryptic reference to the land of Israel. Cf. 11:16, 41, where it is preceded by the word אֶרֶץ (ʾerets, “land”).
verses.commentary:
8:9 "a rather small horn which grew exceedingly great toward the south, toward the east and toward
the Beautiful land" This refers to the fourth Seleucid ruler known as Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175-164
B.C.). We learn from history that he gained, through craftiness (cf. Dan. 8:24), a rather
extensive kingdom and was especially a problem to the Jewish people of Palestine (i.e. "the beautiful land,"
cf. Dan. 11:16,41; Jer. 3:19).

The Hebrew term gdl (BDB 152, KB 178, Qal IMPERFECT with waw)
appears in Dan. 8:8, 9, 10-11. In 8:8 it means "magnified himself"; in 8:9 it means "grew exceedingly great,"
as it does figuratively in 8:10, "it grew great." It is obvious that at least two senses are possible.

- arrogance, Dan. 8:8,10,11

- size, extent, Dan. 8:9.10

It is hard to know which is the intent of the original author.

▣ "south. . .east. . .in the Beautiful Land" It is possible from secular history to document the
nations that Antiochus IV attacked.

- south ‒ Egypt (Daniel 11)

- east ‒ Parthia

- Beautiful Land ‒ Canaan/Palestine (cf. Dan. 11:16,41)

verses.zh: 它渐渐强大，高及天象，将些天象和星宿抛落在地，用脚践踏。
verses.en: It grew so great it reached the army[NOTE:1] of heaven, and it brought about the fall of some of the army and some of the stars[NOTE:2] to the ground, where it trampled them.
notes: Traditionally, “host.” The term refers to God’s heavenly angelic assembly, which he sometimes leads into battle as an army.

In prescientific Israelite thinking the stars were associated with the angelic members of God’s heavenly assembly. See Judg 5:20; Job 38:7; Isa 40:26. In west Semitic mythology the stars were members of the high god’s divine assembly (see Isa 14:13).
verses.commentary:
8:10 "to the host of heaven" The PREPOSITION "to" is translated in poetry as
"as far as," "even to," or "up to" (cf. Dan. 8:11).

The term "host" often applies to YHWH"s angelic army (TEV, cf. Josh. 5:14,15; 1 Sam. 1:3;
Neh. 9:6), but in this context (cf. Dan. 8:12) it refers to

- the people of God ("saints," cf. Dan. 7:18,22,27)

- imagery for the little horn's ambition to rival God (e.g., Isa. 14:13, the kings of Babylon),
in which case the stars would refer to angels or heaven

It is problematic that in the span of four verses this term (BDB 838) is used in several
senses.

- "the host of heaven," Dan. 8:10 (faithful believers or angels)

- "the commander of the host," Dan. 8:11 (angels)

- "the host," Dan. 8:12 (believers)

- "the host," Dan 8:13 (believers or temple worshipers and temple servants)

Here is where context is crucial. Hebrew, being such an ancient language, uses terms in several
ways (semantic field). Our problem as modern interpreters is that we demand specific historically verifiable
details and consistent, lexical usage. The genre and our distance in time from the actual events make
these demands impossible. This is a faith document, not a history book!

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF ANGELIC BEINGS

SPECIAL TOPIC: holy ones

▣ "and some of the stars to fall to the earth" Who does this refer to?

- Usually in Jewish extra-biblical apocalyptic literature falling stars refer to angels coming to earth, but in this context
"stars" is a parallel to "hosts" (the people of God, cf. Dan. 8:24a; 12:3; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS); therefore,
this idiom is referring to the earlier promises of God that Israel will be like
the stars of heaven (in number, cf. Gen. 15:5; Jer. 33:22; in glory, cf. Dan. 12:3).

- This verse refers to the little horn of the third kingdom attacking God's people (i.e., those faithful Jews who opposed
Antiochus' laws), as did the little horn of the fourth kingdom in Dan. 7:21,25. There is an anti-God force loose in creation.
It can be identified by its attack on God, God's Messiah, and God's people! Here, "stars" could refer to "the holy ones" (i.e., the faithful).

verses.zh: 并且它自高自大，以为高及天象之君；除掉常献给君的燔祭，毁坏君的圣所。
verses.en: It also acted arrogantly against the Prince of the army,[NOTE:1] from whom[NOTE:2] the daily sacrifice was removed and whose sanctuary[NOTE:3] was thrown down.
notes: The prince of the army may refer to God (cf. “whose sanctuary” later in the verse) or to the angel Michael (cf. 12:1).
Or perhaps “and by him,” referring to Antiochus rather than to God.
Here the sanctuary is a reference to the temple of God in Jerusalem.
verses.commentary:
8:11 "It even magnified itself to be equal with the Commander of the host" One characteristic
of these Gentile kings has been their arrogance. The influence of the fall (cf. Genesis 3) continues!

The phrase "to be equal" is the same PREPOSITION as "up to the hosts" in
Dan. 8:10.

"The Commander" is the Hebrew word (BDB 978) for "chief," "ruler," "official," "captain,"
or "prince." This could refer to:

- YHWH, Dan. 8:11c, 25

- Messiah, possibly Dan. 8:11; 7:13-14

- a powerful angel, Dan. 8:13; 10:1-9

- Michael, Israel's national angel, Dan. 10:13,31; 12:1

The next few phrases seem to imply either #1 or #2.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

▣ "it removed the regular sacrifice from Him and the place of His sanctuary was thrown down" This
seems to refer to something involving the daily morning and evening sacrifices in the temple ritual called
"the continual" (cf. Exod. 29:38-42; Num. 28:1-8) and/or all the sacrificial system. This daily ritual was stopped ("removed," BDB 926, KB 1202,
Hophal PERFECT; which is the Qere reading.

The second VERB, BDB 1020, KB 1527, Hophal PERFECT, may
refer to the same event) by Antiochus IV Epiphanes and he further defiled the temple by regularly offering a swine on the altar
and placing an image of Zeus in the Holy Place (cf. Dan. 11:31; 12:11). Antiochus IV tried to Hellenize the Jews (cf. I Macc. 1.54-61;
II Macc. 4.11-6.11) by forcing them to eat the flesh of swine. This caused the rebellion led by the priest of Moden, whose son, Judas
Maccabees, through an extended guerilla warfare, finally succeeded in defeating the Seleucid army and, in 165 B.C.,
cleansed and restored the temple. In modern times, this is known as the Festival of Lights (Hanukkah) , and is celebrated in December
(the date changes each year because the Jews use a lunar calendar).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SACRIFICIAL SYSTEMS OF THE ANE

verses.zh: 因罪过的缘故，有军旅和常献的燔祭交付它。它将真理抛在地上，任意而行，无不顺利。
verses.en: The army was given over,[NOTE:1] along with the daily sacrifice, in the course of his sinful rebellion.[NOTE:2] It hurled[NOTE:3] truth[NOTE:4] to the ground and enjoyed success.[NOTE:5]
notes: The present translation reads וּצְבָאָהּ נִתַּן (utsevaʾah nittan, “and its army was given”) for the MT וְצָבָא תִּנָּתֵן (vetsavaʾ tinnaten, “and an army was being given/will be given”). The context suggests a perfect rather than an imperfect verb.

Heb “in (the course of) rebellion.” The meaning of the phrase is difficult to determine. It could mean “due to rebellion,” referring to the failures of the Jews, but this is not likely since it is not a point made elsewhere in the book. The phrase more probably refers to the rebellion against God and the atrocities against the Jews epitomized by Antiochus.
Two medieval Hebrew MSS and the LXX have a passive verb here: “truth was hurled to the ground” (cf. NIV, NCV, TEV).
Truth here probably refers to the Torah. According to 1 Macc 1:56, Antiochus initiated destruction of the sacred books of the Jews.
Heb “it acted and prospered.”
verses.commentary:
8:12 "on account of transgression" Some see this as:

- the sins of the Jewish people (cf. Dan. 9:24) which God allowed to be punished by a foreign
leader (cf. Isa. 10:5; Jer. 51:20)

- the sins of Jewish leadership which helped Antiochus

- or more probably in this context, Antiochus IV Epiphanes' sin (cf. Dan. 8:13,23)

I think #3 fits best.

▣ "the host" This seems to refer to the people of God. See note and Special Topics at Dan. 8:10.

▣ "the regular sacrifice" See note at Dan. 8:11.

▣ "it will fling truth to the ground" The "it" here refers to the actions of the little horn.
The same VERB (BDB 1020, KB 1527) appears in v. 11 and in Ezek. 19:12, but the concept is
expressed in Isa. 59:14. In general it refers to the worship of God or the word of God. Notice the little horn
is allowed by YHWH to do this evil.

"Truth" is a significant theological term (BDB 54). It denotes the trustworthiness and faithfulness
of God that can be seen in His faithful followers. Therefore, this could refer to Antiochus' persecution and murder of
faithful Jews during his reign.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND
FAITHFULNESS (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: TRUTH/TRUE

▣ "perform its will and prosper" This refers to fallen humanity's independent attitude,
which is a recurrent theme in Daniel (cf. Dan. 5:19; 8:4; 11:3,16,36). It will succeed (by God's will) but only for a designated
period of time (cf. Gal. 6:7).

verses.zh: 我听见有一位圣者说话，又有一位圣者问那说话的圣者说：「这除掉常献的燔祭和施行毁坏的罪过，将圣所与军旅（或译：以色列的军）践踏的异象，要到几时才应验呢？」
verses.en: Then I heard a holy one[NOTE:1] speaking. Another holy one said to the one who was speaking, “To what period of time does the vision pertain—this vision concerning the daily sacrifice and the destructive act of rebellion and the giving over of both the sanctuary and army to be trampled?”
notes: The holy one referred to here is presumably an angel (cf. 4:13 [10AT], 23 [20AT]).
verses.commentary:
8:13 "I heard a holy one" This is translated "saint" in Dan. 7:18,21,22,25 and refers to faithful
believers. Here it must refer to the conversation between two angels (cf. possibly Dan. 7:27) for Daniel's
benefit. Other OT titles for angels are

- "sons of God" (cf. Gen. 6:2; Job 1:6; 2:1; 38:7; Ps. 29:1; 89:6-7; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: "sons of God" IN GENESIS 6)

- "holy ones" (cf. Dan. 4:13; Ps. 89:5, 7; Zech. 14:5; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: holy ones)

- "watchers" (cf. Dan. 4:13, 17, 23; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE)

- sometimes "man" or "men" (cf. Dan. 8:15,16; 9:20; 10:5,16,18; 12:6-7; Zech. 1:8,10,19; 2:1,3)

▣ "How long" This does not refer to Jeremiah's prophcy about a seventy year exile (cf. Dan. 9:2;
Jer. 25:11,12; 29:10; Zech. 7:5). It is connected to the "little horn" of the third empire (i.e., Greece,
cf. Dan. 8:21), which is being discussed in Dan. 8:9-14. Therefore, this time frame is related to the
atrocities of Antiochus IV (175-164 B.C.), who desecrated the temple and attempted to force
individual, faithful Jews to become Hellenists.

- The TEV translates this so that the three aspects of the question stand out.

- How long will these things that were seen in the vision continue?

- How long will an awful sin replace the daily sacrifices?

- How long will the army of heaven and the temple be trampled on?

- H. C. Leupold, Exposition of Daniel, p. 352, says that the Hebrew text has four items in apposition to "vision."

- the regular daily offerings

- the crime-causing horror

- the sanctuary to be trodden under foot

- the host to be trodden under foot

▣

NASB
"while the transgression causes horror"

NKJV
"the transgression of desolation"

NRSV
"the transgression that makes desolate"

TEV
"the awful sin"

NJB
"of horrifying iniquity"

REB
"impiety causes desolation"

LXX
"the sin of desolation"

Peshitta
"iniquity and corruption"

This probably refers to the idol of Zeus Olympius, that Antiochus IV placed in the temple
(II Maccabees 6:2). This VERB, "makes desolate" (BDB 1030, KB 1563, Qal
ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) may be a word play from the Canaanite deity, Ba'al Shamem
("Lord of Heaven"), because "heaven" has the same Hebrew consonants as "makes desolate." Zeus was the Greek
counterpart of Ba'al.

This same phrase appears in Dan. 9:27; 11:31; and 12:11. It refers to different atrocities,
but all are connected by rebellion against God and His people. In the Bible it can refer to

- Antiochus IV

- Titus' destruction of Jerusalem in A.D. 70 (Preterists)

- the end-time antiChrist (Futurists)

It is obviously a multiple fulfillment prophecy.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ABOMINATION OF DESOLATION

▣

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta
"the host"

TEV
"the army of heaven"

NJB
"the army"

NEB, REB
"the fairest of all lands"

JPSOA
"the (heavenly) hosts"

The MT has the NOUN "hosts" (BDB 838, cf. vv. 10,11,12,13), which means
"army," "war," or "warfare." BDB suggests this refers to Michael, the angel-prince of Israel (cf. Dan. 12:1) because the Hebrew
is MASCULINE SINGULAR.

However, it could be a collective use of Judah's military (i.e., hosts).

The NEB, REB have a similar Hebrew root, "and of the beauty."

- and of the army ‒ וצבא

- and of the beauty (cf. v. 9) ‒ וצבי

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

verses.zh: 他对我说：「到二千三百日，圣所就必洁净。」
verses.en: He said to me, “To 2,300 evenings and mornings;[NOTE:1] then the sanctuary will be put right again.”[NOTE:2]
notes: The language of evenings and mornings is reminiscent of the creation account in Genesis 1. Since “evening and morning” is the equivalent of a day, the reference here would be to 2,300 days. However, some interpreters understand the reference to be to the evening sacrifice and the morning sacrifice, in which case the reference would be to only 1,150 days. Either way, the event that marked the commencement of this period is unclear. The event that marked the conclusion of the period was the rededication of the temple in Jerusalem following the atrocious and sacrilegious acts that Antiochus implemented. This took place on December 25, 165 b.c. The Jewish celebration of Hanukkah each year commemorates this victory.

Heb “will be vindicated” or “will be justified.” This is the only occurrence of this verb in the Niphal in the OT. English versions interpret it as “cleansed” (KJV, ASV), “restored” (NASB, TEV, NLT), or “reconsecrated” (NIV).
verses.commentary:
8:14

NASB, NKJV, JPSOA, Vulgate
"He said to me""

NRSV, LXX, Peshitta
"he answered him"

TEV
"the other angel answered"

NJB
"the first replied"

REB
"the answer came"

The MT has "and he said to me," but context seems to require "him"
(i.e., two interpreting angels speaking to one another, cf. v. 13).

- to me ‒ אלי

- to him ‒ אליו

The UBS Text Project, p. 312, suggests "to me," but gives it a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

▣ "For 2,300 hundred evenings and mornings" This phrase has been interpreted in
three ways:

- 2300 full days (E. J. Young, pp. 173-175; NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 420, 1. b.)

- a number equivalent to three years, 55 days; this calculation seems to follow the usage in Genesis 1
("evenings and mornings") and the phrase related to persecution in Dan. 7:25

- refers to the number of times "the continual" sacrifice was not given

Context favors #2 because of the use of a similar period of time in Daniel and Revelation. See
note at Dan. 7:25.

Differing commentators choose one. I like #2, but H. C. Leupold, Exposition
of Daniel, p. 355, quotes a German commentator, Meinhold (1889), ". . .an entirely satisfactory
computation has neither been found here nor for the kindred periods in chapters nine and twelve." The
problem is that we forget that this is apocalyptic/prophetic literature, not history.

If one assumes this portion of Daniel is related exclusively to the atrocities of Antiochus IV, then this
identifies the period of time of his persecution of the faithful (i.e., holy wars).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FORTY-TWO MONTHS

▣

NASB, REB
"the Holy Place will be properly restored"

NKJV, JPSOA
"the sanctuary shall be cleansed"

NRSV
"the sanctuary shall be restored to its rightul state"

TEV
"the Temple will be restored"

NJB
"the sanctuary will have its rights restored"

LXX
"the sanctuary shall be purified"

Peshitta
"then righteousness shall prevail"

This VERB, Niphal PASSIVE (BDB 842, KB 100, PERFECT
WITH WAW) is used in this form only here in the OT. The basic meaning is "to be made just or
righteous," so here it would imply, "shall be put in right or properly pure condition." December 12,
165 B.C. was the date of the cleansing and restoration of the temple in Jerusalem by
Judas Maccabeus. See note at Dan. 8:11.

verses.zh: 我―但以理见了这异象，愿意明白其中的意思。忽有一位形状像人的站在我面前。
verses.en: While I, Daniel, was watching the vision, I sought to understand it. Now one who appeared to be a man was standing before me.
verses.commentary:
8:15 "I sought to understand" As the Gentile kings needed Daniel's God-given gift to understand
their dreams, so Daniel needs heavenly beings to help him. Angelic mediation and interpretation is one
of the characteristics of apocalyptic literature. Humans cannot discover truth. It must be revealed!

▣ "who looked like a man" This is the Hebrew word gbr, (BDB 149) which makes up
Gabriel's name. This has nothing to do with Dan. 7:13. Angels often appear in human form (cf. Zech. 1:8,10;
2:1,4). This does not describe their true essence, simply how they appear to us. See note at Dan. 8:13.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE

verses.zh: 我又听见乌莱河两岸中有人声呼叫说：「加百列啊，要使此人明白这异象。」
verses.en: Then I heard a human voice coming from between the banks of the Ulai. It called out, “Gabriel,[NOTE:1] enable this person to understand the vision.”
notes: The only angels whose names are given in the OT are Gabriel (Dan 8:16; 9:21; cf. Luke 1:19, 26) and Michael (Dan 10:13, 21; 12:1; cf. Jude 9; Rev 12:7). The name Gabriel means in Hebrew “man of God,” and Michael means “who is like God?”
verses.commentary:
8:16 "Gabriel" Only two angels are named in the Bible, Gabriel and Michael. Michael is called the
Archangel of Israel (cf. Dan. 10:13,21; 12:1; Jude 1:9; Rev. 12:7), while Gabriel seems to be God's messenger angel
(cf. Dan. 9:21; Luke 1:19,26). His name means "man of God" or "strong man of God" (BDB 150).

verses.zh: 他便来到我所站的地方。他一来，我就惊慌俯伏在地；他对我说：「人子啊，你要明白，因为这是关乎末后的异象。」
verses.en: So he approached the place where I was standing. As he came, I felt terrified and fell flat on the ground.[NOTE:1] Then he said to me, “Understand, son of man,[NOTE:2] that the vision pertains to the time of the end.”
notes: Heb “on my face.”
Or “human one.”
verses.commentary:
8:17 "I was frightened and fell on my face" Humans are shocked at the presence and awesomeness
of the spiritual realm (see NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 692).

- God, Gen. 17:3; Job 13:11,21; Ezek. 1:28; 3:23; 44:4

- angels, Dan. 8:17; 10:9,10,12,15,19; Rev. 1:17

- visions, Job 7:14 (4:13-14); Dan. 7:28; 8:27

▣ "Son of man" Here "man" simply refers to Daniel as a human being (Adam, cf. Dan. 8:16),
as in Ezek. 2:1; 3:1; 4:1; 5:1; 6:2; 7:2; 12:2,8; and Ps. 8:4. The angel Gabriel is addressing Daniel.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF MAN

▣ "understand" This is a Hiphil IMPERATIVE (BDB 106, KB 122), as it is
in Dan. 8:16 (cf. John Joseph Owens, Analytical Key to the Old Testament, vol. 4, p. 737). Gabriel
is commanded by the man above the Ulai Canal (i.e., an angel) to help Daniel understand the conversation
(cf. Dan. 8:15), spoken in the dialogue between the two holy ones (i.e., angels) in Dan. 8:13-14.

There are authoritative levels in the angelic world.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE

▣ "the vision pertains to the time of the end" This vision seems to refer not to the far
future, but the relatively near future (i.e., Empires of Persia and Greece). This should give modern
interpreters a warning about trying to define the phrase "the time of the end" (cf. Dan. 8:19) as always
eschatological (i.e., Dan. 12:4,6; NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 955). In Dan. 11:35,40 "the end time" is used of the
period of Greek rule involving the kingdoms of the Ptolomies and Seleucids (323-165 B.C.).

verses.zh: 他与我说话的时候，我面伏在地沉睡；他就摸我，扶我站起来，
verses.en: As he spoke with me, I fell into a trance with my face to the ground. But he touched me and stood me upright.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “on my standing.”
verses.commentary:
8:18 "I sank into a deep sleep" The presence of the spiritual realm causes humans to be frightened
and pass out (BDB 922, KB 1191, cf. Gen. 15:12; Job 4:13; Dan. 10:9). In Rev. 1:17 John looked as if he
had died!

▣ "he touched me" The angel's touch was a great comfort (cf. Dan. 10:10,16,18; possibly 9:21;
1 Kgs. 19:7; Rev. 1:17). The spiritual realm can manifest physicalness.

Just an added thought about angels in the physical realm. In modern times there have appeared
physical forms of flying objects (i.e., UFOs). I have become convinced these are fallen angels' attempt to lead modern
naturalists away from God and His unique revelation (i.e., in His book, and in His Son). Modern secularists ask, "Are we
alone in the universe?" No, we are not! The angelic world has several levels and categories (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE). Some are supportive of mankind, made in God's image and likeness,
but some are not (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: DEMONS [fallen angels]).

Let me list some helpful books in this area of modern deception.

- William M. Alnor, UFO in the New Age (1992)

- William M. Alnor, UFO Cults and the New Millennium (1992)

- Gary Bates, Alien Intrusion (updated and expanded), (2010)

- a good YouTube video by Walter Martin, "UFOs ‒ Friend, Foes, or Fantasy"

▣ "made me stand upright" Exactly why the angel wanted Daniel to stand up (BDB 763, KB 840, Hiphil
IMPERFECT with waw) is uncertain, but it happens again in Dan. 10:11 (Qal
IMPERATIVE). Perhaps it has to do with the dignity of faithful followers made in God's image.
Angels seem so powerful to humans in this time period and this fallen reality, but in truth, humans have great dignity
and worth. See full exegetical note at Hebrews 1:14 online.

verses.zh: 说：「我要指示你恼怒临完必有的事，因为这是关乎末后的定期。
verses.en: Then he said, “I am going to inform you about what will happen in the latter time of wrath, for the vision[NOTE:1] pertains to the appointed time of the end.
notes: The Hebrew text does not actually state the referent (the vision Daniel saw in vv. 8-12; cf. also v. 13), which has been specified in the translation for clarity. Some Greek witnesses add “the vision” here.
verses.commentary:
8:19 "the final period of the indignation" This term (BDB 276) is used often in Isaiah of YHWH's
indignation against His people for their covenant faithlessness; therefore, He punishes them by means
of foreign nations (cf. Isa. 10:5-6,25; 13:2-16 [esp. v. 5]). However, His indignation will pass
(cf. Isa. 26:20; 30:27; 66:7-24 [esp. v. 14]). This theme is continued in Ezekiel (cf. Ezek. 21:31;
22:24,31). It is foreshadowed in Deut. 28:49-57.

In the context of the book of Daniel, this indignation (BDB 276) has to do with the
independence and arrogance of the Gentile nations who God used to judge His people. Their arrogance
is projected into the distant future (i.e., Greece for Dan. 8:19 and a future (at least future to Daniel) antichrist for 11:36
[cf. Dan. 7:8,20-22,23-26; 2 Thessalonians 2; Revelation 12-13]). Now He will judge these Gentile nations (cf. Dan. 11:36).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SECOND COMING, IV.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTICHRIST

▣ "for it pertains to the appointed time of the end" This phrase (BDB 417) is found
here and in Dan. 11:27,29,35, which all refer to events relating to Greece, especially Antiochus IV, who
aggressively attacks God's people.

The confusion so common in interpreting Daniel is the failure to:

- recognize its genre and to try to identify all details historically

- recognize its near future symbols and its far future symbols

- the little horns of Dan. 7:8

- Dan. 9:1-23 vs. 9:24-27

- Dan. 11:1-35,40-45 vs. 11:31-39

- recognize its merging of anti-God kingdoms. The fourth kingdom is Rome (Preterism), but more, it is all
Gentile world-dominating powers (Idealism).

verses.zh: 你所看见双角的公绵羊，就是玛代和波斯王。
verses.en: The ram that you saw with the two horns stands for the kings of Media and Persia.
verses.commentary:
8:20 "the ram. . .Media and Persia" The ram was the sign of Persia (Aries, the Zodiac sign), but
the ram was also the guardian spirit of Persia and the king wore the ram's emblem to battle.

verses.zh: 那公山羊就是希腊王（希腊：原文是雅完；下同）；两眼当中的大角就是头一王。
verses.en: The male goat[NOTE:1] is the king of Greece,[NOTE:2] and the large horn between its eyes is the first king.
notes: Heb “the he-goat, the buck.” The expression is odd, and the second word may be an explanatory gloss.
Heb “Javan.”
verses.commentary:
8:21 "the shaggy goat. . .Greece" In Dan. 8:5 there is a Hebrew CONSTRUCT for male
goat (BDB 862 and 777). In Dan. 8:21 there are two words which the Handbook on the Book of Daniel,
from the Untied Bible Societies, says is made up of the Hebrew word for male goat (BDB 972 II) and the
Aramaic word for he-goat (BDB 862), which are in opposition, p. 222. The ADJECTIVE form
of this term means "hairy," therefore, the additional word "shaggy" in Dan. 8:21. This additional term
usually refers to the goats offered as a sin-sacrifice (cf. Lev. 4:23,24; 9:15; 16:5,7-8; Num. 7:16).

The goat was the Zodiac sign of Greece, Capricorn, and it was the national symbol of the
Macedonian coat of arms. These two verses are very historically specific in the identification of the
second and third Gentile kingdoms of Daniel's vision.

▣ "the first king" This is obviously Alexander the Great.

verses.zh: 至于那折断了的角，在其根上又长出四角，这四角就是四国，必从这国里兴起来，只是权势都不及他。
verses.en: The horn that was broken[NOTE:1] and in whose place there arose four others stands for four kingdoms that will arise from his nation, though they will not have his strength.
notes: Heb “the broken one.” The word “horn” has been supplied in the translation to clarify the referent.
verses.commentary:
8:22 "although not with his power" None of the rival Greek generals (satraps) ever equaled the power
and extent of Alexander's kingdom!

verses.zh: 这四国末时，犯法的人罪恶满盈，必有一王兴起，面貌凶恶，能用双关的诈语。
verses.en: Toward the end of their rule, when rebellious acts[NOTE:1] are complete, a rash[NOTE:2] and deceitful[NOTE:3] king will arise.[NOTE:4]
notes: The present translation reads הַפְּשָׁעִים (happeshaʿim, “the rebellious acts”) for the MT הַפֹּשְׁעִים (happosheʿim, “the rebels”). While the MT is understandable (cf. NIV, “when rebels have become completely wicked”), the filling up of transgressions is a familiar OT expression (cf. Gen 15:16) and fits this context well. Cf. the LXX, Theodotion, the Vulgate, and the Syriac.
Heb “strong of face.”

Heb “understanding riddles.” Possible meanings include “double-dealing” (BDB 295 s.v. חִידָה; cf. TEV, CEV) and “with a good knowledge of intrigue” (HALOT 309 s.v. חִידָה; cf. NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT).
Heb “stand” or “stand up.”
verses.commentary:
8:23-26 These verses are in poetic form in the NASB, NRSV, NJB, and REB translations. This means interpreters
should note the parallelisms.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

8:23 "A king will arise, insolent and skilled in intrigue" This seems to describe Antiochus IV
Epiphanes' rise to power. Therefore, in this context, "in the latter period" must refer to the latter time of the Greek Empire.

▣

NASB
"insolent and skilled in intrigue"

NKJV
"who understands sinister schemes"

NRSV
"skilled in intrigue"

TEV
"stubborn, vicious and deceitful"

NJB
"ingenious-minded man"

REB
"a master of strategem"

JPSOA
"impudent and versed in intriuge"

LXX, Peshitta
"who understands obscure sayiings"

This is literally "strong of face" (CONSTRUCT BDB 738 and 815) and
"one who understands riddles" (CONSTRUCT BDB 106 and 295). Antiochus IV applied wisdom in a
negative way, only to achieve his own ends!

The non-canonical, interbiblical books of I, II Maccabees record this periof of history.

verses.zh: 他的权柄必大，却不是因自己的能力；他必行非常的毁灭，事情顺利，任意而行；又必毁灭有能力的和圣民。
verses.en: His power will be great, but it will not be by his strength alone. He will cause terrible destruction.[NOTE:1] He will be successful in what he undertakes.[NOTE:2] He will destroy powerful people and the people of the holy ones.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “extraordinarily he will destroy.”
Heb “he will succeed and act.”

See the corresponding Aramaic expression in 7:27. If the “holy ones” are angels, then this probably refers to the angels as protectors of God’s people. One could translate, “people belonging to (i.e., protected by) the holy ones.” If the “holy ones” are God’s people, then this is an appositional construction, “the people who are the holy ones.” One could translate simply “holy people.” For examples of a plural appositional genitive after “people,” see 11:15, 32. Because either interpretation is possible, the translation has deliberately preserved the ambiguity of the Hebrew grammar here.
verses.commentary:
8:24 "his power will be mighty, but not by his own power" Here again, is the recurrent theme
of God's control and direction of human history (cf. Dan. 8:25f; 2:20-23). God used Assyria, Babylon,
Persia, Greece, Rome, and will use whomever He chooses to accomplish His will (cf. Romans 9)! Often humans,
even redeemed humans, do not understand (cf. Isa. 55:8-11).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SECOND COMING, IV.

▣

NASB
"he will destroy to an extraordinary degree"

NKJV, LXX
"he shall destroy fearfully"

NRSV
"shall cause fearful destruction"

TEV, Peshitta
"will cause terrible destruction"

NJB
"will plot incredible schemes"

REB
"he will work havoc untold"

JPSOA
"he will be extraordinarily destructive"

The first VERBAL (BDB 810, KB 927) is a Niphal PARTICIPLE
and the second VERB (BDB 852 II, KB 1026) is a Hiphil PERFECT with
waw. This word is often used for the wonders and marvelous works of God (cf. Exod. 15:11; Isa. 25:1;
29:14; Dan. 12:6). Here, however, it speaks of the terribly destructive acts of this king of the third
empire (cf. Dan. 8:11-13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW GRAMMAR

▣ "And prosper and perform his will" See note at Dan. 8:12.

▣

NASB
"will destroy mighty men"

NKJV, JPSOA, Peshitta
"shall destroy the mighty"

NRSV, NJB, LXX
"shall destroy the powerful"

TEV
"will bring destruction on powerful men"

REB
"will work havoc on the mighty nations"

The VERB means

- "corrupt" (BDB 1007, KB 1469, Hiphil PERFECT with waw, cf. Gen. 6:12;
Deut. 4:16; 31:29; Ezek. 16:47)

- "ruin" (cf. Mal. 3:11)

- "destroy" (cf. Dan. 8:25; Isa. 36:10; Jer. 51:20)

The ADJECTIVE "mighty" usually means numerous (BDB 783, cf. "many" of
Dan. 8:25d). Because of Daniel's literary style it is surely possible

- that "the mighty men" and "the holy people" are parallel

- The other option would be to see "mighty men" as the army of national or political rivals.

- The full phrase denotes the king's (i.e., little horn) complete success.

This phrase "the holy people" is literally "the people of the holy ones," which is very
similar to Dan. 7:27. Many scholars believe that the phrase in Dan. 7:27 is parallel to "holy ones" of
Dan. 7:18,22, and 25. In context Dan. 8:24 cannot refer to angels.

SPECIAL TOPIC: holy ones

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF ANGELIC BEINGS

verses.zh: 他用权术成就手中的诡计，心里自高自大，在人坦然无备的时候，毁灭多人；又要站起来攻击万君之君，至终却非因人手而灭亡。
verses.en: By his treachery[NOTE:1] he will succeed through deceit.[NOTE:2] He will have an arrogant attitude,[NOTE:3] and he will destroy many who are unaware of his schemes.[NOTE:4] He will rise up against the Prince of princes, yet he will be broken apart—but not by human agency.[NOTE:5]
notes: The Hebrew term has a primary meaning of “skill, insight,” but here it has the connotation “cunning, treachery.” See BDB 968 s.v. שֵׂכֶל, שֶׂכֶל.
Heb “he will cause deceit to succeed by his hand.”
Heb “in his heart he will act arrogantly.”

Heb “in peace.” The Hebrew word used here is difficult. It may refer to the security felt by those who did not realize the danger of imminent attack, or it may refer to the condition of being unaware of the impending danger. The latter idea is reflected in the present translation. See further, BDB 1017 s.v. שַׁלְוָה.
Heb “with nothingness of hand.”
verses.commentary:
8:25 This fits what we know of Antiochus IV. See also I Maccabees 1:29-41,44-50; 4:38-39.

▣ "He will magnify himself in his heart" The VERB (BDB 152, KB 178) is
a Hiphil IMPERFECT (i.e., continuing action). This has been the recurrent problem of fallen humanity and
especially of tyrannical dictators and potentates. This activity always attracts God's attention
(cf. Genesis 11; Isa. 9:9; 10:12; Dan. 5:20; 8:11; 11:36-37).

▣

NASB
"while they are at ease"

NKJV
"in their prosperity"

NRSV, TEV
"without warning"

NJB, JPSOA
"taking them unawares"

REB
"when they least expect it"

LXX
"be deceit"

Peshitta
"suddenly"

The term "at ease" (BDB 1017) means quietness in the sense of security, but without
warning at such a time and in such a place (probably "the Beautiful Land," i.e., Palestine,
cf. Dan. 8:9,11,16,41), they will be attacked (cf. Dan. 11:21,24).

The attacker will be the king of Dan. 8:23 and those attacked will be "the mighty men and
the holy people" of Dan. 8:24.

▣ "he will even oppose the Prince of princes" The VERB, "will even oppose" (BDB 763, KB 840) is
a Qal IMPERFECT.

This same word, "prince" (BDB 978, cf. Dan. 8:11,25; 10:13,21; 12:1)
is translated "commander" in 8:11 and seems in context to refer to YHWH (cf. Josh. 5:12-15). The Hebrew
word does not imply a crown prince, co-regent, or ruler in waiting as it does in English, but the chief
leader. It is used of

- the Messiah in Isa. 9:6,7

- Michael the Archangel (cf. Jude 9)

- Israel in Dan. 10:13,21; 12:1

The redundant "Prince of princes" is a Hebrew SUPERLATIVE, "the greatest of all rulers"
(i.e., King of Kings, cf. 2:37,47; Ezek. 26:7; or [God of gods]; Ezra 7:12).

▣ "But he will be broken without human agency" The VERB (BDB 990, KB 1402) is a
Niphil IMPERFECT. This is the recurrent theme of God's sovereignty and control of history
(cf. Dan. 2:20-23).

verses.zh: 所说二千三百日的异象是真的，但你要将这异象封住，因为关乎后来许多的日子。」
verses.en: The vision of the evenings and mornings that was told to you is correct.[NOTE:1] But you should seal up the vision, for it refers to a time many days from now.”

verses.commentary:
8:26 "evenings and mornings" This refers to the offering of a lamb in the temple each morning and
evening (i.e., "the continual," cf. Dan. 8:11-14,19). The Jewish culture starts the new day at evening, following the order of
Gen. 1:5,8,13,19,23,31.

The vision and prophecy of chapter 8 is future to Daniel, but past to us. This gives us
a great opportunity to evaluate prophetic/apocalyptic language in a known event (cf. D. Brent Sandy,
Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic,
pp. 103-128). We can read I Maccabees, Josephus, and secular histories to compare how the event was
recorded in the Bible and outside the Bible. The differences show us

- the stylized language of Hebrew prophecy

- the over-the-top emotional hyperboles of apocalyptic symbolism

verses.zh: 于是我―但以理昏迷不醒，病了数日，然后起来办理王的事务。我因这异象惊奇，却无人能明白其中的意思。
verses.en: I, Daniel, was exhausted[NOTE:1] and sick for days. Then I got up and again carried out the king’s business. But I was astonished at the vision, and there was no one to explain it.
notes: The Hebrew word here is נִהְיֵיתִי (nihyetiy). Its meaning is not entirely clear. Hebrew הָיָה (hayah) normally has meanings such as “to be” or “become.” Here, however, it describes Daniel’s emotional and physical response to the enigmatic vision that he has seen. It is parallel to the following verb, which refers to illness, and seems to refer to a state of utter exhaustion due to the amazing things that Daniel has just seen. The LXX lacks the word. On the meaning of the word see further, BDB 227-28 s.v. הָיָה Niph.2, and DCH 2:540 s.v. היה I Ni.3.

You can hear my four audio tapes on the recapitulation model for understanding
Revelation. Click on "Worldwide Voices" (yellow box) on my homepage, then my name,
and A. #3.

- As in his first vision Daniel was compelled to focus on the fourth kingdom; two years later (compare Dan. 7:1 with 8:1) God further
revealed information about the second and third kingdoms in another vision. Daniel's visions are not chronological.

The little horn of the third kingdom is focused on because it (he) will impact the lives and worship of Israel more than
any other previous Gentile ruler.

The little horn of the fourth kingdom will also impact God's people in the future.

- first coming temporal judgment of

- Jerusalem and the temple (Preterism)

- Nero

- Roman Empire

- an end-time world ruler (Futurism)

- The language has switched back to Hebrew because Daniel, chapters 8-12 are messages for God's people. This vision
is primarily about the future suffering and domination caused by the little horn(s) against God's people. For them, the vision is
about a limited time of suffering and desecration followed by a divine intervention.

The twenty-three hundred evenings and mornings (cf. Dan. 8:14) were a sure promise of the deliverance and
restoration of the temple/Jerusalem (i.e., the small rebuilt temple of Zerubbabel, Joshua, and Haggai).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FORTY-TWO MONTHS

- The book by D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic,
has been very helpful and I recommend it to all who attempt to understand Daniel 7-12. He even gives a whole chapter on the
interpretation of the apocalyptic imagery of Daniel 8, pp. 101-128.

The other book that has been so helpful in understanding the different genres of the Bible is How to Read the Bible For
All Its Worth by Gordon Fee and Doug Stuart.

As interpreters our worst enemies are:

- western culture and evangelical Christianity's over-emphasis on literalism

- a systematic eschatology (usually personally unexamined), which has been given to us by sincere, godly, well-meaning
parents, pastors, denominations, and authors (Futurism)

- Satan does not know God's plans; therefore, he must have an anti-God leader prepared and active in every age (cf. 1 John 2:18)
to carry out his bidding (Idealist). Antiochus IV is one example of a selfish, self-centered, atheistic individual who wants, not only
political and military power, but also adoration, even worship, and there have been many others throughout human history like him.
Fallen humanity regularly produces this type of individual. Yet, God is still sovereign and He even uses these kinds of persons
to accomplish His will, as He does Satan.
